nodes.description: Mice lacking CYP26C1 develop without an evident embryonic phenotype; combined loss of CYP26A1 and CYP26C1 causes anterior brain truncation and loss of migratory cranial neural crest cells. Facial skin is not described in the cited abstract.

evidence.reference_title: CYP26A1 and CYP26C1 cooperatively regulate anterior-posterior patterning of the developing brain and the production of migratory cranial neural crest cells in the mouse.
evidence.snippet: Furthermore, Cyp26a1-/-Cyp26c1-/- mice fail to produce migratory cranial neural crest cells in the forebrain and midbrain.

nodes.description: The lesions consistently lie on an oblique line from the preauricular region to the angle of the mouth, matching the embryonic fusion line between the maxillary and mandibular prominences. Incomplete ectodermal fusion along this line has been proposed as the developmental defect, by analogy with membranous aplasia cutis congenita. The proposal rests on lesion distribution and histology; no developmental study has observed it.

nodes.description: In the mouse embryo Cyp26c1 is expressed in the maxillary and mandibular components of the first pharyngeal arch and along the line where these prominences fuse, the site of the FFDD4 skin lesions. Its proposed role is to shield these tissues from retinoic acid during facial development, so loss of CYP26C1 is thought to expose the fusion line to excess retinoic acid signaling. This step is inferred from expression data and enzyme function; it has not been demonstrated in a model that reproduces the human lesion.

nodes.description: Lesional skin in the focal facial dermal dysplasias shows a thin, flattened epidermis, replacement of the dermis by loose connective tissue, reduced and fragmented elastic fibers, and absence of adnexal structures and subcutaneous tissue, resembling membranous aplasia cutis congenita. These descriptions come mostly from clinically diagnosed cases across the FFDD types.

nodes.description: CYP26C1 hydroxylates all-trans, 9-cis and 13-cis retinoic acid and the active metabolite 4-oxo-all-trans retinoic acid, converting them to polar products. Loss of CYP26C1 activity is expected to reduce clearance of these active retinoids in the tissues where it is expressed. Retinoic acid levels have not been measured in FFDD4 patients or tissue.
